summary: Generation tools transformed production while training-data litigation transformed the business relationship with AI.

analysis.body:
The Information sector, which covers media and publishing businesses, recorded 45.0% of firms using AI in the latest survey period, up from 41.9% the prior period, making it one of the more active adopters among tracked industries. That figure reflects the practical reality: generation tools have moved into everyday production workflows, touching everything from article drafting and image creation to audio and video editing, and the pace of uptake has continued to climb rather than plateau.

Where the documented activity concentrates most heavily right now, however, is not in tooling but in legal risk. The US Copyright Office is conducting a multi-part study covering three distinct questions that matter directly to media businesses: whether AI-generated content can be registered, how training on copyrighted material should be treated, and what protections should exist around digital replicas of real people. That study is the primary legal reference for the sector, and its conclusions will shape what media companies can own, license, and prohibit.

Running alongside the regulatory process is a wave of litigation that touches every major content category the sector produces. Training-data cases involving news publishers, musicians, and visual artists are all active, and the docket status of each is being tracked in real time. The combination of an unsettled copyright framework and live lawsuits means that media companies face genuine uncertainty about both the content they feed into AI systems and the content those systems produce on their behalf.

For a decision-maker weighing deployment, the operational case for generative tools is already established enough that adoption is measurably rising, but the legal infrastructure around those tools is still being written. The Copyright Office study and the outcome of ongoing litigation will determine whether training practices used today remain permissible and whether AI-assisted outputs can be protected as intellectual property. Deploying without tracking both tracks, the regulatory and the judicial, carries real exposure.
